title: Nothing new
hook: there is no new thing under the sun (Ecclesiastes 1:9)
tomorrow: what happens when you throw your bread on the water?

segments.voice: Yesterday, vanity of vanities: the Preacher looked at everything he'd built and called it hevel, breath. Brief, not worthless. Today he looks up from his own life to the whole sky.

Read a parent's letters from when they were your age, or an old diary, and there's a jolt: the same worries, almost word for word. Is that bad news, or a relief? The Preacher stands outside and watches. The sun rises, sets, and hurries back to where it rose. The wind goes south, turns north, circles round. "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full." Then he says it: "there is no new thing under the sun."
screen: `THE SAME WORRIES, WORD FOR WORD.` → `THE SUN HURRIES BACK.` → `NO NEW THING UNDER THE SUN.`

segments.voice: On its own, that sounds tired. But look at the line just before the sun: "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever." The people change. The ground holds. So Qoheleth's nothing new cuts two ways. It humbles: your crisis isn't the first, and the book says plainly that former things aren't remembered. And it steadies: whatever you're walking through, others walked this ground and it held them. Now a neighbor who says something close. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor and Stoic, wrote in his private notebook that whoever has seen the present has seen everything, all that has been and all that will be, since all things are of one kind and one form. Same sun, two windows. And the honest difference: Marcus finds his peace in the reason that runs through nature, and in doing his duty inside it. Qoheleth's book ends somewhere else: "Fear God, and keep his commandments," and meanwhile eat your bread as God's gift. Neither is the other in disguise. The teaching, plainly: in Ecclesiastes, nothing new is a humbling truth and a comfort at once, because the earth that outlasts you also held everyone before you.
screen: `THE EARTH ABIDETH.` · `IT HUMBLES, AND IT STEADIES.` · `MARCUS: SEEN THE PRESENT, SEEN ALL.` · `TWO WINDOWS, TWO ENDINGS.` · then, large: `NOTHING NEW.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you do that people before you did too: a recipe, a song, the way you fold laundry, even a worry. Hold the people who did it before you in mind, one generation behind another. For a minute, let the old pattern carry you, instead of you carrying it.
Nothing new: the sun, the wind and the rivers going round, and the earth holding still under all of it.
Here's the line: nothing new; someone stood exactly here before, and the ground held. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ecclesiastes is read as wisdom literature in Jewish and Christian tradition; its 'under the sun' passages sit within a book that closes on the call to fear God and keep the commandments. Marcus Aurelius's Meditations voices a similar view of the world's repeating patterns.
